analysis:
Reviewed the memory-admission changes in ProviderLoop+ModelLoading.swift and the startup-preload hook in ProviderLoop+StartupPreload.swift. The PR adds retained-KV-segment credit to reclaimableMemoryBytes (lines 1333-1342), an evictionCanReach helper, a releaseReclaimableMemoryForLoad() path that calls GlobalKVCacheBudget.releaseRetainedKVSegments() followed by a cache clear (1347-1350), and a reclaimBeforeSkip closure wired into the startup preloader (StartupPreload.swift:244-245). These changes affect only local memory-admission and eviction arithmetic and availability: when to evict an idle model, when to reject fast, and when to skip a preload. They do not touch the coordinator WebSocket contract, attestation, key custody, authorization or encryption.

The release credit is applied only to feasibility decisions and is not counted after the release, so it does not over-admit loads. Eviction is still gated by evictableModelSlots (no in-flight requests, reservations, pins or unloading), and unloadModel(forEviction:) rechecks those conditions. The load-time recheck, post-load headroom guard and post-bridge guard are unchanged in kind.

Threat-model fit: T-028 (residual GPU/KV data) and T-041 (prefix-cache) are the nearest threats. Releasing retained free KV segments and clearing the MLX cache does not weaken them; it frees memory sooner. The SSD cache tier, its HMAC names, TTL and KEK handling are not modified here. Availability threats T-010 and T-029 are not worsened.

Integration questions that remain: the implementations of GlobalKVCacheBudget.releaseRetainedKVSegments, CBv2RetainedKVSegments, ModelLoadAdmission.evictionCanReach and the StartupPreloader reclaimBeforeSkip semantics are outside the supplied evidence. I could not verify that releasing retained segments cannot disrupt in-flight requests on busy engines. The code comments say engines drop them at their next step, and this is not a security-boundary issue in the supplied code. No concrete security regression identified.
